standard.title: Write sourced historical arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments, using historical knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence from sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments using historical knowledge, concepts and terms that reference evidence from sources (AC9HH7S08). They can construct basic historical writing with source references. They have not yet applied structural elements for argumentative effect (introduction with explicit argument, conclusion that restates and summarises), presented findings across multiple formats, or applied historical concepts and terms with precision in their appropriate historical context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and historical arguments — using structural elements for argumentative effect, applying historical terms and concepts in their appropriate context, referencing source evidence, and presenting findings in formats appropriate to audience and purpose.

nodes.label: Historical terms and concepts in context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply historical terms and concepts in their appropriate historical context — using the vocabulary of the discipline accurately to describe, explain and argue about the past.
nodes.minimum_width: Accurate use of at least four historical terms or concepts in their appropriate historical context within a piece of writing.
nodes.typical_width: Historical terminology used precisely and in context across the range relevant to Y8 History: continuity, change, significance, turning point, cause, effect, perspective, interpretation, primary source, secondary source, evidence; period-specific terms (feudalism, papacy, caliphate, bushido, deva-raja, ariki, Encomienda, conquistador). Terms used to do analytical work, not just as vocabulary decoration.
wider: Review a piece of historical writing and identify where terms are used decoratively vs analytically — practising the distinction between naming a concept and using it to advance an argument
Examine how historians use period-specific vocabulary to signal precision and credibility — and practise incorporating such terms into explanations where they add meaning rather than complexity
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate use of historical terminology is prerequisite to disciplinary writing. Students who misuse or omit key terms cannot construct precise historical arguments, and imprecise use of concepts such as cause, continuity and significance undermines the logic of their writing.

response_modes.reason: Precise use of historical terms requires repeated practice in varied writing contexts. Students commonly use terms loosely or interchangeably (e.g. 'cause' and 'reason', 'continuity' and 'tradition'). Build precision through sustained writing practice with feedback.

success_criteria: Uses at least four historical terms or concepts accurately in their appropriate historical context
Uses terms analytically — to make a point or advance an argument — rather than as mere labels

nodes.label: Structural elements for argumentative effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use structural elements — an introduction that outlines an argument and a conclusion that summarises and restates it — to communicate historical explanations or analysis with argumentative effect.
nodes.minimum_width: A piece of historical writing with an identifiable introduction that outlines an argument and a conclusion that summarises and restates it.
nodes.typical_width: Historical writing with deliberate structural design: an introduction that states the argument (not just the topic) and signals the reasoning to follow; body paragraphs that develop the argument with evidence; a conclusion that restates the argument in light of the evidence presented. The structure as a rhetorical tool, not just an organisational container.
wider: Compare two introductions to the same historical question — one that states a topic and one that states an argument — and explain why the second is more effective for historical writing
Practice writing conclusions that go beyond summary — adding a statement of significance or connecting the historical argument to a broader question about the period

response_modes.reason: Students often confuse introducing a topic with introducing an argument. Scaffold the distinction: an argument-introduction states a claim that will be supported by evidence; a topic-introduction merely announces what will be discussed. The structure signals the reasoning, not just the content.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The distinction between a topic-introduction and an argument-introduction is a transferable writing skill that extends well beyond History. Students who master this in historical argument will apply it across disciplines — making this node unusually high-value for developing academic writing generally.
success_criteria: Writes an introduction that outlines a specific historical argument (not just a topic) with reference to the evidence that will support it
Writes a conclusion that summarises and restates the argument in light of the evidence presented

nodes.label: Presenting findings across formats
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can present historical findings or knowledge in a range of formats — such as a podcast, oral presentation or essay — appropriate to the audience and purpose, with reference to evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Historical findings presented in at least one format (not necessarily written) with appropriate reference to evidence.
nodes.typical_width: Historical writing across multiple formats: the conventions of different formats (essay vs podcast vs oral presentation vs annotated timeline); how evidence is referenced differently in spoken vs written formats; how audience and purpose shape choices about what to include, emphasise and omit; the consistent requirement to reference evidence regardless of format.
wider: Develop the same historical argument for two different formats (e.g. an essay and a podcast script) and identify what changes and what stays the same — showing how format shapes but does not determine the argument
Examine how historical documentaries or museum exhibits communicate historical knowledge and argument, and evaluate their effectiveness against the criteria applied to written historical argument

response_modes.reason: Presenting across formats integrates all prior skills — terminology (Node 1), argument structure (Node 2), source referencing (from S03–S04) — in a context where the student must make conscious choices about how to adapt disciplinary practices to different communicative contexts.

success_criteria: Presents historical findings in a format appropriate to the audience and purpose, with reference to evidence
Applies historical concepts and terms accurately within the chosen format
